summary:
Amanar, an Amiazighs' nomads name for the Orion constellation, which litterally means “the guide,” is also the name of our browser-based mission control game that puts players in charge of a complete space mission. One of the missions is LUNA-01, where a player moves through a briefing, picks an observation target among NASA’s candidate Artemis south-pole regions, builds the spacecraft, and runs the mission live. Power, heat, communications and data compete for the same limited resources, and random events such as a solar storm or a lost signal force decisions under pressure. A debrief then shows what each choice cost, and a multiverse replay lets players explore the paths they did not take, and see the choices leading to the most optimal result.
Around this core, Amanar adds co-op multiplayer rooms with voice and text, mini-lectures with questions that award badges, and a VR mission control room where the player follows the rover on the lunar surface.
It addresses the challenge by turning abstract engineering trade-offs into consequences players experience. It matters because high-fidelity mission control training costs millions and Amanar offers a free, accessible place to fail, learn and ask “what if?”
details:
Project name: Amanar

What it does and how it works
Amanar is an educational game about exploring the lunar south pole. One of its missions, LUNA-01, asks players to design and fly an orbiter mission whose goal is to find water ice. The player starts with a limited budget and limited resources (energy, heat). They choose the orbit and the rover’s landing site. Then they work through a series of mini-levels, each with multiple-choice options that carry advantages and drawbacks. Every choice affects the budget and resources, so players must manage them throughout. The aim is to collect as much scientific data as possible while using as few resources as possible. At the end, the game gives a score and an educational debrief that explains the consequences of the player’s choices. The hub offers three experiences: the LUNA-01 Orbiter (solo or with a crew of up to 4), the Lunar Rover, and the Training Academy. A guest co-op mode lets friends create or join a mission without an account.

The VR Lunar Rover Simulation provides a WebGL and WebXR-powered driving experience set at the Lunar South Pole. Utilizing high-resolution NASA topographic elevation datasets, realistic low-sun polar lighting, and pre-optimized 3D spacecraft assets, players sit directly in the rover's mast camera cockpit with an interactive 3D HUD tracking speed, battery reserve, and terrain pitch. We decided to add this feature to fulfill the core NASA Space Apps VR challenge requirement by delivering an immersive visual payoff—allowing players to transition from high-level mission control planning to directly testing their custom rover's navigation across hazardous, permanently shadowed lunar craters.

The Space Mission Operations Academy is a gamified 5-chapter educational module containing interactive mini-lessons, visual dynamic tools, and a 50-question QCM dataset covering space environment physics, Keplerian orbital mechanics, spacecraft subsystems, ISS rendezvous, and debris sustainability. Featuring instant green/red answer feedback, physics solution explanations, and an 8/10 score threshold to unlock progressive chapters and digital commander badges, it structures player learning step-by-step. We decided to add this feature to ground the game in authentic aerospace engineering principles, equipping players with the real-world STEM knowledge required to optimize their resource trade-offs and make evidence-driven decisions during mission design.

Benefits of our project

  • Makes space mission design accessible to anyone, with no technical background needed.
  • Teaches real mission trade-offs (budget, energy, data, risk) through play rather than lectures.
  • Can be played solo or with a team, and the learning stays optional so players can simply enjoy the game.

Intended impact
We want to spark curiosity about space exploration and help students and the general public understand what it takes to run a real mission, inspired by recent NASA efforts such as Artemis and the search for lunar water ice. The goal is for players to learn by deciding, not by memorizing, and to build the teamwork and decision-making skills that real missions demand.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React and Vite
  • Backend: Node.js with a TypeScript simulation engine and an HTTP API, plus WebSockets for real-time multiplayer
  • Shared engine: the UI and the backend use the same mission-calculation engine, so results are consistent
  • DevOps: Docker and Docker Compose, Nginx for serving the production build, automated tests, and deployment on Vercel
  • Data and inspiration: NASA public resources, including the Curiosity rover dataset, and the JPL Concept Maturity Levels framework for structuring the mission stages

Creativity

  • Players design the mission themselves instead of following a fixed storyline.
  • Unexpected events and challenges make each playthrough different.
  • Several missions share the same decision-and-resource structure, so the game can grow easily.
  • A final certification and quiz, based on what the player learned, give the game an educational layer that sets it apart from other space games.
  • Planned AI-generated challenges will make every session unique (see below).

Future development and scalability

  • Mars mission (Curiosity): a new mission inspired by the Curiosity rover. It uses the same structure, with mission design first and then mini-level tasks, and it draws on NASA’s Curiosity data to choose a landing site, plan the rover’s route, and manage energy and data.
  • ISS astronaut missions: simulations of real astronaut missions aboard the International Space Station, where players take on crew roles and handle daily operations, experiments, and emergencies.
  • Group play: extending the current co-op mode so that players can team up with others in shared missions, with each player responsible for part of the decisions, and so that teams can race each other.
  • AI-generated challenges: challenges created by AI during the game to test the player’s decision-making skills. They would adapt to the player’s choices, resources, and progress, so that no two missions play out the same way.

Factors we considered

  • Fun first: learning is never forced, so players stay free to explore and have fun.
  • Realism vs. accessibility: the mission numbers are illustrative, not NASA/GMAT-validated, so the game stays simple while still reflecting real trade-offs.
  • Teamwork: solo and co-op play (1 to 4 players) with no accounts, to keep joining easy.
  • Reliability and maintainability: a shared engine, automated tests, and containerized deployment.
  • Replayability and scalability: varied missions, random AI-generated challenges, and an architecture that makes it easy to add new missions.
